title: The Salvadoran Jesuits (1989)
hook: six Jesuits and two women killed at a university in San Salvador

segments.voice: Yesterday, magis: the more, measured by love and not by hours. Your line was magis. Where did a little more care turn out to be more, and where was it just busier? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-six.

A university campus in San Salvador, during a civil war. The Jesuits who run it live in a house on the grounds. They are professors: a philosopher, a psychologist, a sociologist, theologians, and an older priest who works with schools for the poor. A woman named Elba Ramos cooks and keeps house for them, and on this night she and her daughter Celina are sleeping there, in a room of the house. Before dawn, soldiers come through the gate. Today we stay with them, quietly, and ask what kind of teaching gets a person killed.
screen: `A CAMPUS IN A CIVIL WAR.` → `PROFESSORS, A COOK, HER DAUGHTER.` → `SOLDIERS BEFORE DAWN.`

segments.voice: The Salvadoran Jesuits. That night, soldiers of the Salvadoran army killed six Jesuit priests at the Central American University, along with Elba and Celina Ramos. A United Nations truth commission later investigated and named the military as responsible. The rector was Ignacio Ellacuría, a philosopher. With him died Ignacio Martín-Baró, a psychologist; Segundo Montes, a sociologist; Amando López; Juan Ramón Moreno; and Joaquín López y López. Why them? Not because they carried weapons. They carried research, lectures and public arguments. Their university had spoken out about the poor, and about the suffering of ordinary people in the war, and it had pressed for a negotiated peace. For some in power, that teaching was dangerous. This is where the last few days come home. Cura personalis, the whole person, stretched to a whole people. God in all things, including a country's poorest neighborhoods. The magis, asking what a university is for. These men had decided the answer included telling the truth out loud. And Elba and Celina are a reminder that the dead were not only the famous ones. In John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Today, people come to the campus to pray where they died. The point is not drama. It's that teaching matters. Telling the truth in a classroom can cost something, in some places still.
screen: `SOLDIERS, A CAMPUS, EIGHT LIVES.` · `THEY CARRIED LECTURES, NOT WEAPONS.` · `THE WHOLE PERSON, A WHOLE PEOPLE.` · `ELBA AND CELINA, NOT ONLY THE FAMOUS.` · then, large: `GREATER LOVE THAN THIS NO MAN HATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember teachers under threat. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a teacher who mattered to you, then widen the circle: teachers, journalists, students, anyone in the world right now who tells the truth in a place where that is dangerous. You don't need their names. Hold them, and Elba and Celina too, for a few slow breaths. If you pray, you can pray for their safety and their courage, or say the names you heard today one by one. If you don't, simply keep them in mind with respect. The bell holds the time.
The Salvadoran Jesuits. Six priests and two women killed at their university in San Salvador, remembered for teaching the truth about the poor during a war. Today's word.
Your line: killed for teaching. Today, thank one teacher, past or present, by name, in a message or in your heart. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics, and especially Jesuit schools and universities, remember the Salvadoran Jesuits and Elba and Celina Ramos with Masses, vigils and prayers for peace and justice.
